subject: Renal
subtopic: Nephrotic syndrome: minimal change, FSGS, membranous, amyloid, diabetic
vignette: A 4-year-old boy has 2 weeks of periorbital edema and frothy urine. He had an upper respiratory infection 10 days ago. Labs show heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperlipidemia. Light microscopy shows normal glomeruli, immunofluorescence is negative, and electron microscopy shows effacement of podocyte foot processes.
question: Which of the following best describes this patient's renal disease?

options.text: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis — segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis with foot process effacement
Minimal change disease — normal light microscopy with foot process effacement, often primary and steroid-responsive
Membranous nephropathy — diffuse GBM thickening with granular spike-and-dome subepithelial deposits
Amyloidosis — Congo red apple-green birefringence with mesangial expansion
Diabetic glomerulonephropathy — nodular (Kimmelstiel-Wilson) glomerulosclerosis

explanation_correct: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and is often primary (idiopathic), triggered by a recent infection, immunization, or other immune stimulus (the '4 Is'); rarely it is secondary to lymphoma via cytokine-mediated injury. Light microscopy is normal (lipid may be seen in proximal tubule cells), immunofluorescence is negative, and electron microscopy shows effacement of podocyte foot processes. It is typically steroid-responsive. These findings and the pediatric age make it the best answer.

explanation_incorrect.A: FSGS shows segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis on light microscopy rather than normal glomeruli, is more common in Black patients and in HIV/sickle cell/obesity, and often progresses to CKD.
explanation_incorrect.C: Membranous nephropathy shows diffuse capillary and GBM thickening with granular immune-complex deposition and subepithelial spike-and-dome deposits on electron microscopy, not normal glomeruli.
explanation_incorrect.D: Amyloidosis would show amorphous deposits with apple-green birefringence on Congo red stain and mesangial expansion, not isolated foot process effacement in a child.
explanation_incorrect.E: Diabetic glomerulonephropathy shows mesangial expansion, GBM thickening, and eosinophilic nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions) and would not be expected in a healthy 4-year-old.

educationalObjective: Minimal change disease causes pediatric nephrotic syndrome with normal light microscopy, foot process effacement, and steroid responsiveness.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Nephrotic syndrome: minimal change, FSGS, membranous, amyloid, diabetic
vignette: A 34-year-old Black man with HIV presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria and a rising serum creatinine over 6 months. Renal biopsy shows segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis of some glomeruli with foot process effacement; immunofluorescence is negative except for nonspecific focal IgM and C3.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Minimal change disease with normal glomeruli and diffuse foot process effacement
Membranous nephropathy with diffuse GBM thickening and spike-and-dome deposits
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, which may be secondary to HIV and can progress to CKD
AA amyloidosis with Congo red apple-green birefringence
Diabetic glomerulonephropathy with Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules

explanation_correct: FSGS can be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to HIV infection, sickle cell disease, obesity, or congenital malformations, and it is more common in Black people. Biopsy shows segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis with podocyte foot process effacement; immunofluorescence is often negative but may show nonspecific focal IgM, C3, and C1. It frequently progresses to CKD, matching this patient's rising creatinine.

explanation_incorrect.A: Minimal change disease has normal glomeruli on light microscopy and negative immunofluorescence, without the segmental sclerotic and hyalinotic lesions seen here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Membranous nephropathy is defined by diffuse GBM thickening and subepithelial spike-and-dome deposits rather than segmental sclerosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Amyloidosis would show amorphous mesangial deposits that are Congo red positive with apple-green birefringence, which is not described here.
explanation_incorrect.E: Diabetic glomerulonephropathy shows diffuse mesangial expansion and nodular sclerosis in a patient with long-standing hyperglycemia, not segmental lesions in association with HIV.

educationalObjective: FSGS is a cause of nephrotic syndrome that can be secondary to HIV, sickle cell disease, or obesity and may progress to CKD.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Nephrotic syndrome: minimal change, FSGS, membranous, amyloid, diabetic
vignette: A 58-year-old man with long-term NSAID use for arthritis develops nephrotic syndrome. Renal biopsy shows diffuse capillary loop and GBM thickening; immunofluorescence is granular, and electron microscopy reveals subepithelial deposits with a spike-and-dome appearance. He also has a right leg DVT. Serology is positive for anti-PLA2R antibodies.
question: Which of the following best identifies the disease and explains his increased thrombotic risk?

options.text: Minimal change disease, in which hypoalbuminemia alone accounts for thrombosis
FSGS secondary to NSAIDs, with thrombosis from associated advanced CKD
Amyloidosis, with thrombosis due to nephrotic-range protein loss
Membranous nephropathy, which is associated with an increased risk of thromboembolism including renal vein thrombosis
Diabetic glomerulonephropathy, in which hyperglycemia drives a prothrombotic state

explanation_correct: Membranous nephropathy (membranous glomerulonephritis) can be primary, as with antibodies to phospholipase A2 receptor (anti-PLA2R), or secondary to drugs such as NSAIDs, penicillamine, and gold; infections such as HBV, HCV, and syphilis; SLE; or solid tumors. It shows diffuse GBM thickening with granular immune-complex deposition and subepithelial spike-and-dome deposits. It carries an increased risk of thromboembolism, including DVT and renal vein thrombosis, which explains his DVT.

explanation_incorrect.A: Minimal change disease has normal light microscopy and no immune deposits; it is not associated with anti-PLA2R antibodies or a spike-and-dome pattern.
explanation_incorrect.B: FSGS shows segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis rather than diffuse GBM thickening, and is not the classic nephrotic syndrome linked to renal vein thrombosis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Amyloidosis is diagnosed by Congo red apple-green birefringence and mesangial expansion, not granular subepithelial deposits or anti-PLA2R antibodies.
explanation_incorrect.E: Diabetic glomerulonephropathy shows nodular (Kimmelstiel-Wilson) sclerosis with mesangial expansion and would not produce granular spike-and-dome deposits or anti-PLA2R antibodies.

educationalObjective: Membranous nephropathy shows diffuse GBM thickening with granular spike-and-dome deposits and is linked to thromboembolism and anti-PLA2R antibodies.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Nephrotic syndrome: minimal change, FSGS, membranous, amyloid, diabetic
vignette: A 63-year-old man with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has progressively worsening edema and nephrotic-range proteinuria. Kidney biopsy shows amorphous eosinophilic material expanding the mesangium; Congo red stain demonstrates apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Immunofluorescence is positive for AA protein.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Amyloidosis (secondary AA type), with the kidney as the most commonly involved organ
Minimal change disease, with normal glomeruli and foot process effacement
Membranous nephropathy, with granular subepithelial deposits
FSGS, with segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis
Diabetic glomerulonephropathy, with Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules

explanation_correct: Amyloidosis is associated with chronic conditions that predispose to amyloid deposition, including AL amyloid (light chains), AA amyloid (seen with chronic inflammation such as rheumatoid arthritis), and prolonged dialysis. The kidney is the most commonly involved organ. Deposition in the mesangium causes mesangial expansion, and Congo red stain shows characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarized light; AA amyloid stains positive for AA protein.

explanation_incorrect.B: Minimal change disease has normal glomeruli on light microscopy with foot process effacement and negative Congo red staining, not mesangial amorphous deposits.
explanation_incorrect.C: Membranous nephropathy shows diffuse GBM thickening with granular subepithelial spike-and-dome deposits, not Congo red positive mesangial expansion.
explanation_incorrect.D: FSGS shows segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis with foot process effacement rather than diffuse amorphous mesangial deposits.
explanation_incorrect.E: Diabetic glomerulonephropathy shows mesangial expansion with eosinophilic nodular sclerosis but not apple-green birefringence or AA protein positivity.

educationalObjective: Renal amyloidosis shows Congo red apple-green birefringence and mesangial expansion, with the kidney being the most commonly affected organ.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Nephrotic syndrome: minimal change, FSGS, membranous, amyloid, diabetic
vignette: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus for 18 years has increasing edema. Labs show albuminuria with an elevated urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and a decline in GFR. Biopsy shows mesangial expansion, GBM thickening, and eosinophilic nodular glomerulosclerosis.
question: Which of the following best identifies the process driving her kidney disease?

options.text: Immune-complex deposition with granular immunofluorescence and subepithelial spikes
Podocyte foot process effacement with normal glomeruli on light microscopy
Segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis attributable to hyperfiltration alone
Amyloid fibril deposition with apple-green birefringence
Hyperglycemia-driven nonenzymatic glycation causing mesangial expansion, GBM thickening, and nodular sclerosis, the leading cause of ESRD in the United States

explanation_correct: Diabetic glomerulonephropathy is the most common cause of end-stage renal disease in the United States. Hyperglycemia causes nonenzymatic glycation of tissue proteins leading to mesangial expansion, GBM thickening, and increased permeability; hyperfiltration causes glomerular hypertrophy and scarring. Biopsy shows mesangial expansion, GBM thickening, and eosinophilic nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions). Look for albuminuria with an increased urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio; ACE inhibitors and ARBs are renoprotective.

explanation_incorrect.A: Granular immune complexes with subepithelial spikes indicate membranous nephropathy, not the nodular sclerosis of diabetic disease.
explanation_incorrect.B: Foot process effacement with normal glomeruli is characteristic of minimal change disease, not long-standing diabetes with nodular lesions.
explanation_incorrect.C: Segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis describe FSGS; diabetic nephropathy instead produces diffuse mesangial expansion and Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules.
explanation_incorrect.D: Amyloid deposition would be Congo red positive with apple-green birefringence, which is not seen in diabetic glomerulonephropathy.

educationalObjective: Diabetic nephropathy results from hyperglycemia-driven glycation and hyperfiltration, producing Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules and albuminuria; ACEi/ARBs are renoprotective.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Nephrotic syndrome: minimal change, FSGS, membranous, amyloid, diabetic
vignette: A 52-year-old man with newly diagnosed lymphoma develops sudden-onset nephrotic syndrome. Renal biopsy shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy, negative immunofluorescence, and diffuse podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy. There are no subepithelial deposits or nodular lesions.
question: Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of this patient's nephrotic syndrome?

options.text: Deposition of antigen-antibody complexes along the GBM producing a granular pattern
A cytokine-mediated, rare secondary form of minimal change disease triggered by lymphoma
Nonenzymatic glycation of matrix proteins from underlying hyperglycemia
Amyloid fibril deposition within the mesangium due to chronic inflammation
Urease-producing bacterial infection causing alkaline urine and tubulointerstitial injury

explanation_correct: Minimal change disease is usually primary (idiopathic), triggered by recent infection, immunization, or another immune stimulus (the '4 Is'), but it can rarely be secondary to lymphoma, thought to be mediated by cytokines causing podocyte injury. The biopsy shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy, negative immunofluorescence, and foot process effacement on electron microscopy with no immune deposits, which is classic for minimal change disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Granular immune-complex deposition along the GBM would indicate membranous nephropathy or an immune-complex glomerulonephritis, not minimal change disease with negative immunofluorescence.
explanation_incorrect.C: Nonenzymatic glycation with mesangial expansion and nodular sclerosis describes diabetic glomerulonephropathy, not normal glomeruli with isolated foot process effacement.
explanation_incorrect.D: Amyloid deposition would show apple-green birefringence on Congo red stain and mesangial expansion, which are absent in this biopsy.
explanation_incorrect.E: Urease-producing bacteria cause struvite stones and alkaline urine, not a nephrotic syndrome with normal glomeruli.

educationalObjective: Rare secondary minimal change disease can occur with lymphoma via cytokine-mediated podocyte injury, with normal light microscopy and foot process effacement.
